Presidential Gubernatorial Omoyele Sowore and others after watching MKO documentary
Human rights activist Omoyele Sowore has called for a separate documentary to honour the pro-democracy activists who fought against the annulment of the 12 June 1993 presidential election, saying their contributions to Nigeria’s democratic struggle deserve to be preserved.
Although he commended filmmaker Ose Oyamendan for his documentary on the late Moshood Abiola, Mr Sowore argued that the activists who challenged the annulment also deserve recognition.
The African Action Congress (AAC) presidential candidate expressed this view in a statement on his X page on Monday following a private screening of the “ MKO” documentary , which he attended alongside PREMIUM TIMES Editor-in-Chief Musikilu Mojeed and others.
He said the film revisited a painful and troubling period in Nigeria’s political history and presented revelations that were both emotional and disturbing.
Mr Sowore said the documentary explored the circumstances surrounding Abiola’s death after he won the 1993 presidential election and examined the political actors who frustrated the people’s democratic choice.
He said: “It is a story of betrayal, greed, cowardice, conspiracy, and the extraordinary cruelty of those who would rather destroy a nation than surrender power. June 12 was not merely an annulled election. It was a monumental crime against the democratic aspirations of the Nigerian people, and its consequences continue to haunt Nigeria today.
“But we must also remember that June 12 was not just about MKO Abiola. It was about millions of Nigerians who refused to surrender their democratic rights, and the countless unsung heroes whose courage made the struggle possible. Their stories deserve to be told in full.”

The Ondo-born politician also expressed hope that the documentary would soon reach a wider audience, giving Nigerians interested in history, democracy and the struggle for justice an opportunity to watch it.
“It is a must-watch! And a new documentary about the real fighters of June 12 is long overdue!”
According to Mr Sowore, one of the documentary’s most striking moments appears in its opening sequence, featuring veteran broadcaster Danladi Bako.
During an interview with Mr Abiola on the Nigeria Television Authority (NTA) programme “Morning Ride”, Mr Bako asks whether he intends to become Nigeria’s president.
“Watching that historic exchange decades later, knowing how the events of June 12 unfolded, was particularly haunting. One particularly striking account came from Bello Buhari, who headed the Legal Department of the then National Electoral Commission (NEC) (as it was then known), led by Professor Humphrey Nwosu.
“Bello was responsible for filing the legal action to counter the Association for Better Nigeria (ABN), led by Arthur Nzeribe, a group widely known to be surreptitiously established and encouraged by General Ibrahim Badamosi Babangida to sabotage the 1993 democratic transition program.”
Mr Sowore also recounted Mr Bello’s account of an extraordinary incident involving the late Philip Umeadi, a prominent lawyer who represented the ABN in the legal battle over the June 12 election.
He said Mr Bello recalled that officials found Mr Umeadi dressed only in a towel at the home of Clement Akpamgbo, who served as Attorney-General of the Federation at the time, amid legal moves to prevent the election.
“That revelation alone speaks volumes about the intrigues, conspiracies, and extraordinary lengths to which powerful individuals allegedly went to frustrate the democratic will of Nigerians. Another remarkable moment came after the screening, when Danladi Bako, whose historic interview with Abiola had opened the documentary, stepped forward to speak about Ken Saro-Wiwa, the Ogoni environmental rights activist who was executed by the military regime of General Sani Abacha in 1995. Bako recounted how he had attempted to interview Ken Saro-Wiwa but was prevented from doing so.
“His account was another reminder of the climate of repression, censorship, intimidation, and fear that characterised military rule in Nigeria. It also underscored the extraordinary risks journalists faced when attempting to document the experiences of those challenging military dictatorship. The connection between Abiola and Saro-Wiwa was particularly striking. Both became victims of an era in which powerful military rulers and multinational criminal corporations like Royal Dutch Shell treated democratic aspirations, environmental justice, and fundamental freedoms as threats to their authority.”
Mr Sowore further said the documentary prompted him to reflect on how people he considered wicked could ascend to the highest offices in Nigeria, singling out former military ruler General Ibrahim Babangida.
He called Mr Babangida a gap-toothed “evil genius” and described his annulment of the 12 June election as a monumental betrayal of the Nigerian people.
According to Mr Sowore, the documentary also brought back troubling memories of the greed, selfishness and disregard for national interest displayed by influential figures in both the military and civilian political circles.
“The documentary also brought back disturbing memories of the selfishness, greed, and unpatriotic conduct of powerful figures within both the military and civilian political establishments, including Olusegun Obasanjo, whose political role during that period deserves continued scrutiny.
“In my view, many of these individuals placed their personal ambitions and political calculations above the democratic aspirations of millions of Nigerians. Most disturbing, however, was the documentary’s examination of the role of the United States’ security and political establishment in the events surrounding Chief MKO Abiola’s death”, he said.
He said the documentary presented an unfiltered account of the involvement and potential complicity of powerful international players.
“To me, the film presents a compelling case for investigating what I believe was one of the greatest conspiracies involving local and international political elites in Nigeria’s history.”
Mr Sowore faulted the documentary for overlooking the immense sacrifices of activists who confronted military rule and sustained the June 12 struggle.
He stressed that the pro-democracy movement extended beyond courtrooms, political gatherings, diplomatic engagements and secret meetings.
He said activists took the struggle to the streets, universities, factories, newsrooms, labour unions, including air traffic controllers, and communities across Nigeria.
He said the movement relied on strikes, mass protests, civil disobedience and underground resistance. The politician also recalled the extraordinary incident in which pro-democracy activists hijacked a Nigerian Airways aircraft.
“Where were the stories of the courageous men and women who risked everything, including their lives, to confront the military dictatorship? Where were Chief Gani Fawehinmi, Dr. Beko Ransome-Kuti, Olisa Agbakoba, Frank Kokori, Ayo Obe, Femi Falana, SAN, Adeola Soetan, Joe Okei-Odumakin, Olusegun Mayegun Snr, Chima Ubani, Abdul Oroh, Bamidele Aturu, Ebun-Olu Adegboruwa San,, Shehu Sani, Clement Nwankwo, Frederick Fasehun, Alfred Rewane, Anthony Enahoro, Abraham Adesanya, Ayo Adebanjo, Bola Ige, Olu Falae, Ndubuisi Kanu, Dan Suleiman and Ayo Opadokun.
“Cornelius Adebayo, John Odigie-Oyegun, Ralph Obioha, Wahab Dosunmu, @Owei Lakemba, Abiodun Aremu, Femi Aborisade, Festus Iyayi, Ojudu Babafemi, Nosa Igiebor, Chris Anyanwu, Kunle Ajibade, Osa Director, Niran Malaolu, Moshood Fayemiwo, George Mba, Ben Obi, Emma Ezeazu, Innocent Chukwuma, Osagie Obayuwana, Felix Tuodolo, Popoola Ajayi, Jerry Yusuf, Alani Akinrinade, Balarabe Musa, Arthur Nwankwo, Ola Oni, Moshood Erubami, Jonathan Ihonde, Igboyako Nowinta, Chukwuemeka Ezeife, Bisoye Tejuoso, Suliat Adedeji, Wale Okuniyi, Richard Akinola, Malcolm Fabiyi, Wale ‘Balo’ Balogun, Aare Gani Adams, Baba Aye, Yinka Odumakin, Abdul Mahmud, Kayode Ogundamisi, Malcolm Fabiyi and countless others whose sacrifices helped sustain the resistance?”
Mr Sowore questioned why the documentary left out Nigerian students who mobilised protests, organised resistance and confronted soldiers in the streets.
He also faulted the filmmakers for excluding the labour movement, whose industrial actions brought the country to a standstill.
He further criticised the documentary’s failure to acknowledge independent media organisations and their practitioners, who endured arrests, detention, harassment, proscription and persecution for challenging military censorship.
Mr Sowore said, “What about the Nigerians in the diaspora who risked their livelihoods, careers, personal safety and everything they had to internationalise the struggle against military dictatorship? And what about the assassinations, attempted assassinations, disappearances, detention, torture and other atrocities that followed the annulment of June 12?
“No doubt the murder of Kudirat Abiola was covered; the assassination of Alfred Rewane was not; the imprisonment of pro-democracy activists, the persecution of journalists, and the brutal repression of ordinary citizens were not footnotes. They were central to the struggle’s history. The June 12 resistance was wild, widespread, courageous, relentless and far bigger than the political personalities who eventually inherited its legacy.”
Mr Sowore stated that the documentary could not adequately capture the resistance against military rule without recognising those who fought it on different fronts, often at risking their freedom and lives in the process.
“This is not to diminish Ose Oyamendan’s important documentary. On the contrary, it is precisely because the documentary is so revealing and consequential that I believe another, even more expansive documentary is long overdue, one that tells the story of the June 12 struggle from the perspective of those who actually fought it, suffered for it and refused to surrender.
“The real fighters of June 12 deserve their own documentary. Their sacrifices must not be erased, forgotten, or appropriated by those who later found themselves in positions of political power.”
Meanwhile, Mr Sowore disclosed that he and Bolaji Abdullahi raised concerns after the screening about the documentary’s portrayal of Bola Ahmed Tinubu as a key figure in the June 12 protest movement.
“We pointed to the absence of documentary evidence showing him participating in even a single day of the street protests. The history of June 12 must be told accurately, without exaggerating the roles of individuals who later became politically powerful.”
The documentary debuted on 1 October at the Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts in Iganmu, Lagos, during activities marking Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary.
Mr Tinubu, Senate President Godswill Akpabio, Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu and presidential Chief of Staff Femi Gbajabiamila attended the premiere.
Mr Tinubu hosted the event alongside First Lady Oluremi Tinubu.
